name: Atrophic Rhinitis
preview_text: The type of dryness tells the story: a parched, desert-like nose with thin crusts points to Lung Dryness; sticky, foul-smelling crusts with bloating suggest Spleen weakness; deep d...
conventional_description: Atrophic rhinitis is a chronic condition in which the nasal mucosa (the lining inside the nose) progressively thins and hardens. The nasal passages can become abnormally wide, yet the person often feels obstructed because of thick, foul-smelling crusts. Typical symptoms include persistent dryness, a constant sensation of stuffiness, loss of smell, and occasional bleeding when crusts are removed. Diagnosis is usually made by an ENT specialist who will look inside the nose and note the pale, thin, dry mucosa and crusting.
conventional_treatments: Conventional management focuses on keeping the nose moist and reducing crusts. This includes regular saline rinses, nasal lubricants like sesame oil or glycerin-based gels, and sometimes antibiotic ointments if secondary infection is present. In severe cases, surgery to narrow the nasal passages may be offered to reduce the drying effect of airflow, though results vary. There is no medication that can reverse the mucosal atrophy itself.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the nose is the opening of the Lungs, and its health depends entirely on a steady supply of fine, mist-like moisture - what we call the clear fluids of the body. These fluids are produced by the Spleen from the food and drink we take in, and their deepest source is the Kidney's Yin essence. When any of these organs falter, the nasal lining loses its nourishment, becomes dry, and begins to atrophy. So atrophic rhinitis is never just a nose problem; it's always a reflection of a deeper organ-level imbalance.
The most direct cause is Lung Dryness, where either external dry weather or internal fluid depletion leaves the Lungs unable to moisten their own orifice. But the Spleen is equally important: if it's weak, it fails to transform fluids, and instead of rising as clear moisture, they pool as dampness below - which is why some people have a dry nose yet also sticky, foul-smelling crusts and digestive sluggishness. The Kidneys come into play when the condition is chronic and deep, with a dry, cracked nose accompanied by night sweats and lower back soreness, signaling that the body's fundamental Yin reserves are running low.
Then there are patterns where heat complicates the picture. Dry-Heat or Dry-Fire can invade the Lung channel, scorching the fluids and causing a burning, inflamed nose with yellow crusts. Damp-Phlegm can obstruct the passages, creating a sensation of stuffiness even though the nasal cavity is wide. And when Qi and Blood are both deficient - often after a long illness - the entire body lacks the raw material to nourish the mucosa, leading to a pale, dry, and empty-feeling nose with overwhelming fatigue. Recognizing which pattern is dominant is the key to effective treatment.
classical_quote: 「鼻槁者，肺热熏灼，津液枯涸，鼻窍失养，致干燥萎缩也。」
classical_translation: "Bi Gao (atrophic rhinitis) occurs when lung heat scorches and burns, causing the body fluids to dry up. The nasal passages lose their nourishment, leading to dryness and atrophy."

tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner first asks about the quality of the dryness. When the nose feels parched and desert-like, with thin, dry crusting and a sense of atrophy, the picture points toward Lung Dryness. The tongue is often red with little coating, and the pulse feels thin and rapid-signs that the Lung’s moisture has been depleted and cannot nourish the nasal passages.
If the dryness comes with sticky, foul-smelling discharge or moist crusts, and the person also struggles with poor appetite, bloating, or loose stools, Spleen Deficiency with Dampness is suspected. The tongue appears pale and puffy with tooth marks and a greasy coat, while the pulse is weak. Here the Spleen fails to transform fluids, leaving dampness to accumulate while the nose remains undernourished.
Intense nasal dryness accompanied by a foul odor, low back soreness, night sweats, and a feeling of heat in the palms and soles suggests Kidney Yin Deficiency with Empty-Heat Blazing. The tongue is red with very little coating, and the pulse is thin and rapid. In this pattern, the Kidney’s yin cannot reach upward, and the resulting empty-heat rises to the Lung, worsening the atrophy and odor.
When the nose feels burning hot, the mucosa looks red and cracked, and yellowish crusts form, Dry-Heat or Dry-Fire is likely. The tongue is red with a yellow coating and the pulse is rapid. Less common patterns, such as Damp-Phlegm in the Lungs (chronic obstruction with sticky phlegm) or Qi and Blood Deficiency (pale, dry tissues with deep fatigue), are considered when the dominant clues don’t fit the more frequent presentations.

patterns.symptoms: ["Nasal dryness with crusting", "Burning sensation in the nose", "Dry cough with scanty sticky phlegm", "Dry mouth and throat", "Thirst", "Slight fever or aversion to wind"]
patterns.worse_with: Dry, hot weather or indoor heating, Spicy, fried, or drying foods, Smoking or smoky environments, Windy, arid weather
patterns.better_with: Cool, moist air, Warm, nourishing foods and soups, Adequate rest and sleep
patterns.why_this_happens: The Lungs open into the nose and rely on a fine mist of Body Fluids to keep the nasal passages moist and healthy. When external Dryness invades, it depletes these fluids directly, leaving the nasal mucosa starved of moisture. Over time this causes the tissues to thin, crack, and form dry crusts - the hallmark of atrophic rhinitis. The same dryness often irritates the throat and airways, producing a stubborn dry cough.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with a dry surface and a thin white or thin yellow dry coating. Pulse: floating (浮 fú), and may be rapid (数 shuò) with a fine (细 xì) quality.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Lung Dryness is both an external invasion and an internal deficit of fluids. Dry environments and heating deplete moisture further, while spicy or fried foods generate internal heat that burns up precious Yin. Moist air, rest, and gentle fluids directly replenish what the Lungs have lost, allowing the nasal tissues to heal.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Use a humidifier at home and at work to keep the air moist, especially during dry seasons. Sip warm water or pear juice throughout the day and favor moistening foods like tofu, spinach, and almonds. Avoid smoking and cut back on coffee, alcohol, and spicy or deep-fried foods, which all consume Body Fluids.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Spleen is meant to transform food and fluids into the clear nourishment that rises to moisten the nose. When the Spleen is weak, this process stalls - fluids pool into internal dampness instead of becoming the fine moisture the nasal passages need. The nose then becomes dry, yet the stagnant dampness can produce thick, sticky discharge and a foul odor. The digestive heaviness and bloating you feel are the same dampness weighing down your middle.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale and swollen with teeth marks, white greasy coating, moist surface. Pulse: soggy (Ru) and slow (Huan), often soft and lacking force.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: The Spleen’s ability to transform fluids depends on warmth and gentle movement. Cold, raw, and greasy foods, as well as damp weather, overwhelm the Spleen, creating more internal dampness while the nose remains dry. Warmth, small meals, and rest support the Spleen’s function, helping it generate the clear moisture that travels upward to soothe the nasal passages.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Favor warm, cooked foods like congee, soups, and stews; avoid cold, raw, greasy, and dairy-heavy meals that burden the Spleen. Gentle daily movement - a walk after meals - helps Qi flow and dries dampness. Use a saline nasal spray to keep the nose comfortable without creating more dampness.

patterns.pattern_name: Kidney Yin Deficiency With Empty-Heat Blazing
patterns.symptoms: ["Dry nose with foul-smelling crusts", "Night sweats", "Five-palm heat (palms, soles, chest)", "Lower back soreness and weakness", "Tinnitus or dizziness", "Dry throat, worse at night"]

patterns.why_this_happens: Kidney Yin is the deepest source of moisture in the body. When it runs low, the upper orifices-especially the nose-lose their natural lubrication, leading to the dryness, thinning, and atrophy that define this condition. At the same time, the depleted Yin fails to anchor the body's Yang, allowing empty-heat to rise and scorch the nasal passages. This heat bakes lingering secretions into foul-smelling crusts and deepens the sensation of dryness and obstruction.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin, and dry with little or no coating, possible cracks. Pulse: fine (细 xì) and rapid (数 shuò).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Yin is easily consumed by overwork, late nights, and sexual excess, while spicy and hot foods stir up empty-heat. These habits directly worsen the underlying deficiency and the rising heat that scorches the nose. Rest, cooling moist foods, and gentle movement help rebuild Yin fluids, anchor Yang, and calm the empty-heat, allowing the nasal passages to stay lubricated and comfortable.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize deeply nourishing, moistening foods: pears, black sesame, walnuts, goji berries, and bone broths. Avoid spicy, fried, or drying foods that fuel empty-heat. Go to bed early-rest before midnight is the best way to replenish Kidney Yin. Gentle exercise like walking or tai chi helps fluid circulation without depleting reserves.

patterns.why_this_happens: When dry-heat invades the Lung channel, it scorches the body's fluids and inflames the nasal passages-the Lung's direct opening. The heat makes the mucosa red and swollen, while the dryness robs it of moisture, leading to cracking, crusting, and a raw burning sensation. This pattern often triggers acute flare-ups of atrophic rhinitis during dry, hot weather or after exposure to heated indoor air.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red and dry, often with cracks; thin dry yellow coat (may be thin white and dry early on); the tip is redder. Pulse: floating and rapid, with the right cun (Lung) position notably large or overflowing.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Dry-heat consumes the body's fluids and inflames the Lung channel, which directly opens into the nose. Cool, moist air and hydrating foods replenish fluids and counteract dryness, while spicy or heating substances add fuel to the fire. Rest allows the body to preserve Yin and fluids, whereas stress and overexertion generate more internal heat, worsening the burning and crusting.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Drink plenty of room-temperature or slightly cool fluids like pear juice, chrysanthemum tea, or lily bulb soup. Avoid spicy, fried, and barbecued foods, as well as alcohol and coffee. Use a humidifier at home, and rinse the nose with a gentle saline spray to keep crusts soft. Rest during acute flare-ups.

patterns.why_this_happens: When the Spleen is weak, it fails to transform and transport fluids, leading to the accumulation of Dampness. This Dampness congeals into Phlegm, which rises and obstructs the Lungs and nasal passages. The sticky Phlegm causes a sensation of nasal stuffiness even when the nasal cavities are widened, and as it stagnates, it dries into foul-smelling crusts that are difficult to clear.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with teeth marks and a thick, white, greasy coating. Pulse: slippery (hua), like beads rolling under the finger; may also feel soggy.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Dampness and Phlegm are heavy, sticky pathogens that worsen with cold, raw, and greasy inputs, which further impair the Spleen's ability to transform fluids. Warmth and drying foods help the Spleen Qi rise and transform Phlegm. Light exercise moves Qi, which helps to disperse Dampness and open the chest and nasal passages.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that burden the Spleen and generate Dampness. Favor warm, cooked meals with mild spices like ginger and cardamom. Gentle daily exercise, such as walking, supports Spleen Qi and helps move phlegm. Keep the home dry and well-ventilated.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Qi and Blood are deficient - often after a long illness, poor diet, or chronic overwork - the body lacks the raw materials to nourish and moisten its tissues. The nasal mucosa is especially sensitive to this depletion: without enough Qi to transport fluids and enough Blood to provide moisture, the lining becomes pale, thin, and dry. This leads to the hallmark crusting, loss of smell, and a widened but empty-feeling nasal cavity, while the whole body shows signs of deep fatigue and pallor.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale body, may be thin or show teeth marks, with a thin white coating. Pulse: fine (thin) and weak.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi and Blood are the fundamental building blocks that nourish every tissue, including the delicate nasal lining. Rest and warm, nutrient-dense foods build them up, while overwork, stress, and cold raw foods drain them further. By protecting and replenishing Qi and Blood, the nose receives the moisture and vitality it needs to heal.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked, easily digestible foods that build Qi and Blood, such as chicken soup, rice porridge with red dates, and lightly cooked leafy greens. Avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that strain the Spleen. Prioritize consistent, restful sleep and gentle daily movement like walking or qigong - never to the point of exhaustion.

faqs.question: Can TCM really help a dry, crusty nose?
faqs.answer: Yes. By addressing the root - whether it's Lung dryness, Spleen weakness, or Kidney Yin deficiency - herbal formulas and acupuncture work to restore the body's ability to produce and distribute moisture to the nasal passages. This is different from simply adding moisture from the outside with sprays. Many patients find that as their internal balance improves, the nose becomes naturally more comfortable and crusts diminish.

faqs.question: How long does it take to see results?
faqs.answer: Most people notice less crusting and a more moist sensation within 4-6 weeks, though deeper deficiency patterns may take 3-6 months for full rebuilding. Acupuncture sessions are typically weekly, and herbs are taken daily. The timeline depends on how long the condition has been present and which pattern is dominant - your practitioner will give you a more personalized estimate after diagnosis.

faqs.question: Can I combine TCM with my saline rinses or nasal ointments?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. TCM treatment works from the inside out and can be safely combined with external moisturizing methods. In fact, keeping the nose clear of crusts with gentle saline rinses can help the herbal medicine work better. Inform your TCM practitioner about everything you're using, and continue any prescribed conventional treatments unless your doctor advises otherwise.

faqs.question: What changes will I need to make to my diet?
faqs.answer: Dietary adjustments are an important support. You'll generally be advised to favor moistening, nourishing foods like pears, honey, lily bulb, black sesame, and soups, while avoiding drying foods such as spicy dishes, deep-fried items, and excessive dairy, which can promote dampness and phlegm. Your practitioner will tailor these recommendations to your specific pattern.

faqs.question: Is acupuncture painful?
faqs.answer: Most people find acupuncture deeply relaxing. Points near the nose, like Yingxiang (LI-20), may produce a brief, mild sensation, but it's not painful. Many patients look forward to their sessions as a time of rest and restoration, and the needles are extremely fine - far thinner than those used for injections.

faqs.question: Can TCM help if I've lost my sense of smell?
faqs.answer: Yes. Loss of smell in atrophic rhinitis is often due to the mucosa being so dry and crusted that odors can't reach the olfactory nerves. As treatment restores moisture and reduces crusting, smell often returns gradually. The improvement may be slow, especially if the atrophy has been long-standing, but many patients do regain some or all of their sense of smell over several months.
